[This indicates that Hell is on the surface of the earth, and Allah knows its place, and where it is in relation to the earth.] [[The addition is from the marginal notes of al-Jamal, quoting al-Qurtubi.]] He said, "Tell me more." It said, "Jibril, peace be upon him, stands before Allah, his muscles trembling. From every tremor Allah creates a hundred thousand angels. Those angels stand before Allah, exalted is He, with their heads bowed. When Allah permits them to speak, they say, 'There is no god but Allah.'" This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows, none shall speak except one whom the Most Gracious permits, and he shall say what is right.﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 184]] meaning the saying, "There is no god but Allah."

Al-Zajjaj said: His saying (Qaf) means "the matter has been decided," as it is said of (Ha Mim), meaning "the matter has been decreed."

Ibn 'Abbas said: (Qaf) is one of the names of Allah, exalted is He, by which He swears. He also said: it is one of the names of the Qur'an. This is also the view of Qatadah. Al-Qurazi said: it is the opening of the names of Allah: Qadir (Capable), Qahir (Subduer), Qarib (Near), Qadi (Judge) and Qabid (Withholder). Al-Sha'bi said: it is the opening of the surah. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: its meaning is, "Stop at Our command and Our prohibition, and do not exceed them." Muhammad ibn 'Asim al-Antaki said: it is the nearness of Allah to His servants, as shown by His saying, ﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein.﴾ Ibn 'Ata' said: Allah swore by the strength of the heart of His beloved Muhammad ﷺ, since he bore the address and it did not affect him, because of the elevation of his state.

(The glorious Qur'an): that is, the exalted in rank. It was also said: the noble, as al-Hasan said. It was also said: the abundant, derived from abundance of worth and station, not from abundance of number, from the saying "So-and-so is abundant among souls." From this is the Arab proverb: "In every tree there is fire, and al-Markh has become glorious." [[Al-Markh and al-'Ifar are two trees containing fire that is not found in other trees; their branches are shaped into firesticks and struck to produce a spark.]] (and al-'Ifar). That is, these two kinds have accumulated more fire than the rest of the trees, according to Ibn Bahr.

The answer to the oath has been said to be: ﴿We know what the earth diminishes of them,﴾ with the lam of emphasis understood, meaning "We have indeed known." It was also said to be: ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder,﴾ and this is the choice of al-Tirmidhi Muhammad ibn 'Ali, who said: (Qaf) is an oath by a name which is the greatest of the names that came forth to the servants, which is Power. He also swore by the glorious Qur'an. Then he recounted what came forth from Power: the creation of the heavens and earths, the provision of servants, the creation of the sons of Adam, the description of the Day of Resurrection, Paradise and Hell. Then He said: ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart.﴾ So the oath falls upon this statement, as if He said: "Qaf, by Power and the glorious Qur'an, I have sworn that in what I have related in this surah there is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while he is present." Ibn Kaysan said: its answer is ﴿what is uttered of speech.﴾ The people of Kufa said: the answer to this oath is ﴿Nay, they wonder.﴾ Al-Akhfash said: its answer is omitted, as if He said, "Qaf, by the glorious Qur'an, you will surely be resurrected," indicated by ﴿When we have died and become dust?﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves.﴾ The (an) is in the accusative position, with the implied sense "because a warner came to them from among themselves," meaning Muhammad ﷺ. The pronoun refers to the disbelievers, and it was also said to refer to both believers and disbelievers together. Then He distinguished between them by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the disbelievers said,﴾ and He did not say "and they said." Rather, He disparaged their state and their action and described them with disbelief, as you say: "So-and-so came to me and made me hear what I disliked," and "The wicked man said to me, 'You are such-and-such.'"

(This is a strange thing!) The 'ajib is the matter at which one wonders. Likewise 'ujab with a damma, and 'ujjab with a shaddah is more common, and likewise u'juba. Qatadah said: their wonder was that they were called to one God. It was also said: it was from their being warned of resurrection and rising. What the Qur'an explicitly states is preferable.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When we have died and become dust?﴾ Here "we shall be raised" is implied, so there is an ellipsis.

(That is a far return.) The rajc is return. That is, it is a far return, meaning impossible. It is said: "I returned him, I return him, a return," and "he returned, he returns, a returning." There is another ellipsis here, meaning: "And they said, 'Shall we be raised when we have died?'" The mention of resurrection, though not repeated here, occurs in many places, and the Qur'an is like a single surah. Also, the mention of resurrection is implied in His saying, ﴿Nay, they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves,﴾ because a warner warns only of punishment and reckoning in the Hereafter.

(We know what the earth diminishes of them): that is, what it eats of their bodies, so nothing is lost to Us, until restoring them becomes difficult for Us. In the revelation: ﴿He said, "What of the former generations?" He said, "Their knowledge is with my Lord, in a Book. My Lord does not err, nor forget."﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 205]] In the authentic hadith: "Every son of Adam is eaten by the earth except the coccyx, from which he was created and in which he will be reassembled." This has been mentioned before. It is also established that the earth does not eat the bodies of the prophets, the friends of Allah and the martyrs; Allah has forbidden the earth to eat their bodies. We have explained this in the book (al-Tadhkirah), and it has also been mentioned earlier in this book.

Al-Suddi said: the diminishing here is death. He means: "We know of them who dies and who remains, because whoever dies is buried, as if the earth diminishes people." From Ibn 'Abbas: it is those among the polytheists who enter Islam.

(And with Us is a preserved Book): that is, with their number and their names. So (hafiz) is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active). It was said: the Preserved Tablet, meaning preserved from the devils, or in which everything is preserved. It was also said: the Book is an expression for knowledge and enumeration, as you say, "I wrote this against you," meaning "I preserved it." This is abandoning the apparent meaning without necessity. It was also said: "And with Us is a preserved Book for the deeds of the sons of Adam, so that We may call them to account for them."

His saying, exalted is He: (Nay, they have denied the truth): that is, the Qur'an, according to the consensus, as al-Mawardi related. Al-Tha'labi said: "the truth" is the Qur'an. It was also said: Islam. It was also said: Muhammad ﷺ.

(So they are in a confused affair): that is, mixed up. They say at one time "a sorcerer," at another "a poet," and at another "a soothsayer," as said by al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd. Qatadah said: "in disagreement." Al-Hasan said: "in confusion," and the meanings are close. Abu Hurayrah said: "corrupt." From this comes "the trusts of people became corrupt," meaning they were spoiled, and "the religion and the affair became confused." Abu Dawud said:

The religion has become confused, so I prepared for it
one with a high withers and a well-knit shoulder-blade.

[[Al-harik is the withers, and al-katad is the junction of the shoulder blades of a human or a horse.]]

Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Marij is the reprehensible matter. 'Imran ibn Abi 'Ata' related from him: "marij" means "mixed up." He recited:

She went round, so I sought with it her inner parts,
and it fell as if it were a marij branch.

The khawt is a branch. Al-'Awfi related from him: "in a matter of error," which is their saying, "sorcerer, poet, madman, soothsayer." It was also said: "changing." The root of maraj is agitation and unease. It is said: "The affair of the people became confused," "the affair of the religion became confused," and "the ring became confused on my finger" when it became loose from thinness. In the hadith: "How will you be, O 'Abdullah [[This is 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, as in the Musnad of Abu Dawud.]], when you are among a people whose covenants and trusts have become confused, and they have disagreed and become like this and like this?" and he interlaced his fingers. Abu Dawud recorded it, and we have mentioned it in the book (al-Tadhkirah).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 50, verses 6–11:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them?﴾ It is a looking of reflection and contemplation, and that the One who is able to bring it into being is able to bring back creation.

(How We built it) We raised it without pillars. (And adorned it) with the stars. (And there are no cracks in it) "Furuj" is the plural of "farj," which means a split. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qais:

*"With it he blocks her farj from behind"* [The line describes her (the mare's) rear. Its first half is: "She has a tail like the train of a bride."]

Al-Kisa'i said: There is no discrepancy in it, no disagreement, and no rifts.

(And the earth, We spread it out and cast in it firm mountains.) Its explanation has preceded in (al-Ra'd) [See vol. 9, p. 280.]

(And We caused to grow in it of every beautiful pair) That is, of every kind of plant. (Beautiful) That is, good, pleasing to the beholders. Its explanation has preceded in (al-Hajj) [See vol. 12, p. 14.]

(As an insight) That is, We made that an insight by which we point to the perfection of Our power. Abu Hatim said: It is in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning We made that an enlightenment and a reminder of Our power. (And a reminder) is conjoined to it.

(For every servant who turns in repentance) returning to Allah, the Exalted, reflecting upon His power. His saying, Exalted is He: (And We sent down from the sky) That is, from the clouds, (blessed water) That is, abundant in blessing.

(And We caused to grow by it gardens and grain of harvest.) The estimate is: "and the grain of the plant that is harvested," which is every thing that is harvested. This is the saying of the Basran grammarians. The Kufans said: It is from the category of attributing a thing to itself, as one says "masjid al-jami'" (the mosque of the congregation), "rabi' al-awwal" (spring of the first), "haqq al-yaqin" (the truth of certainty), "habl al-warid" (the jugular vein), and similar. This was said by al-Farra'. The original is "al-habb al-hasid," so the definite article was removed and the modified noun was attributed to its modifier. Al-Dahhak said: The grain of the harvest is wheat and barley. It was also said: It is every grain that is harvested, stored, and eaten as sustenance.

(And the palm trees, tall with fruit clusters) It is in the accusative on the basis of the coordination, meaning "and We caused to grow the palm trees," [This is as it appears in the originals; perhaps the correct wording is as al-Samin said: "(wal-nakhla) is in the accusative by coordination, meaning 'and We caused the palm trees to grow', and (basiqat) is a circumstantial accusative."] in response to His saying (and grain of harvest), and (basiqat) is a circumstantial clause. The "basiqat" are the tall ones, as said by Mujahid and Ikrimah. Qatadah and Abdullah ibn Shaddad said: Their "busuq" is their straightness in height. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Level. Al-Hasan, Ikrimah also, and al-Farra' said: Heavy with burdens, pregnant. It is said of a she-goat "basaqat" when she gives birth. The poet said:

*"When we left the abode, it remained ruined, in Qurran, in which are the tall, heavy ones."*

The first meaning is more common and more well known in the language. It is said "basaqa al-nakhlu busuqan" when the palm tree grew tall. He said:

*"For us is wine, though not the wine of grapes, but from the produce of the tall ones, noble in the sky, they have gone tall, and their fruits have escaped the hands of the pickers."*

It is said: "Basaqa fulan 'ala ashabihi," meaning he rose above them. "Absaqat al-naqatu" when the milk fell into her udder before giving birth, so she is "mubsiq," and the she-camels are "mabasiq." Qutbah ibn Malik said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) recite "(basaqat)" with the sad, mentioned by al-Tha'labi. I say: What is in Sahih Muslim from Qutbah ibn Malik, who said: I prayed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led us in prayer, and he recited "Qaf, by the glorious Qur'an," until he recited "and the palm trees, tall." He said: I kept repeating it and did not know what he said, except that it is not permissible to substitute the sad for the sin because of the qaf.

(For it are spathes, arranged in layers.) "Tal'" is the first thing that comes out of the fruit of the palm tree. It is said: "Tala'a al-tal'u tuluean" and "atla'at al-nakhlatu," and its tal' is its kufrra before it splits.

(Nadid) That is, layered, one piece placed upon another. In al-Bukhari, "al-nadid" is the kufrra as long as it is in its sheaths, and its meaning is piled one upon another. When it comes out of its sheaths, it is no longer nadid.

(As provision for the servants) That is, We gave them provision, or in the sense that We caused them to grow as provision, because growth has the meaning of provision, or as an object of purpose, meaning We caused them to grow for their provision. Provision is what has been prepared for benefit. The discussion of it has already preceded.

(And We gave life by it to a dead land.) Thus is the resurrection. That is, from the graves, meaning just as Allah gave life to this dead earth, so He will bring you out alive after your death. The "ka" is in the nominative position as the subject. This meaning has passed in more than one place. [See vol. 1, pp. 177 and 211.] He said "dead" (maytan) because the intended thing is the place; had he said "dead" (maytah), it would have been permissible.

He reminded them of the report of those among the deniers who came before them, and warned them of what seized them. We have mentioned their stories in more than one place when they were mentioned.

(Each of them denied the Messengers) from these denying nations.

This is a rebuke to those who deny the resurrection, and it answers their saying: (That is a far-off return). It is said: "ʿayiytu bil-amr" (I was worn out/baffled by the matter) when you do not know its way.

And We created man, meaning mankind. It was also said that "man" refers to Adam.

(And We know what his soul whispers to him) That is, what stirs in his secret thoughts, his heart, and his inner self. This is a warning against the sins that a person commits in secret. Whoever says that "man" refers to Adam holds that what his soul whispered to him was eating from the tree, and then the meaning is general to his offspring. *Waswasah* (whispering) is the soul's talking to itself, like a hidden speech. Al-A'sha said:

You hear the jingling of ornaments as she turns away,
Like the rustle of the *'ishriq* (a plant) stirred by a wind.[[*'Ishriq* (*kaz* or *burj*): a plant that spreads over the ground with broad leaves and no thorns. Its fruit is a husk which, when the wind blows, splits, so that it rustles and makes a sound, like the noise of a valley, and frightens camels.]]

This has already been discussed in (*al-A'raf*).[[See vol. 7, p. 177.]]

(And We are closer to him than the jugular vein) This is the *habl al-'atiq* (the neck vein), which extends from the throat to the shoulder. There are two such veins, one on the right and one on the left. This meaning was transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas and others, and it is the known meaning in the language. *Habl* (vein) is *al-warid*, and it is attributed to itself because the two words differ. Al-Hasan said: *al-warid* is *al-watin*, a vessel attached to the heart. This is an illustration of nearness, meaning: We are closer to him than the vein of his own body, which is part of him, but not in the sense of physical distance. It was also said: meaning, We have more power over him than the vein, given His dominion over it. And it was said: meaning, We know what his soul whispers to him better than the vein that is part of his own self, because it is a vessel that mingles with the heart, so the knowledge of the Lord is nearer to him than the knowledge of the heart. This meaning was transmitted from Muqatil, who said: *al-warid* is a vessel that mingles with the heart. This nearness is the nearness of knowledge and power. Parts of a human being may hide from one another, but nothing hides from God's knowledge.

His saying, exalted is He: (When the two receivers receive, one sitting on the right and one on the left) That is, We are closer to him than the vein of his neck when the two receivers receive, and they are the two angels assigned to him. That is, We know his circumstances, so We have no need for an angel to inform Us. But they were assigned to him to establish the proof against him and to emphasize the matter upon him. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Qatadah said: "the two receivers" are two angels who receive your deeds, one on your right which records your good deeds, and the other on your left which records your bad deeds. Al-Hasan said: When you die, the scroll of your deeds is folded, and on the Day of Resurrection you will be told: (Read your record; sufficient is your soul against you this day as a reckoner)[[See vol. 10, p. 230.]]. By God, just is the One who made you the reckoner of your own soul.

Mujahid said: God, along with His knowledge of a person's circumstances, has assigned two angels by night and two by day to protect his deeds and record his traces, to establish the proof: one on his right records the good deeds, and the other on his left records the bad deeds. This is His saying, exalted is He: (one sitting on the right and one on the left).

Sufyan said: It has reached me that the recorder of good deeds is trustworthy over the recorder of bad deeds, so when the servant sins, the recorder of good deeds says: "Do not hasten, perhaps he will ask God's forgiveness."

This meaning was also transmitted from the hadith of Abu Umamah, who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "The recorder of good deeds is on the right side of a man, and the recorder of bad deeds is on his left. The recorder of good deeds is trustworthy over the recorder of bad deeds. When he does a good deed, the one on the right records it tenfold, and when he does a bad deed, the one on the right says to the one on the left, 'Leave it for seven hours; perhaps he will glorify God or seek forgiveness.'"

It was also transmitted from the hadith of Ali, may God be pleased with him, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The seat of your two angels is on your front teeth,[[In another narration from Ali, may God be pleased with him: "The two angels sit on the molars of the servant..." etc.]] (their pen is your tongue, and their ink is your saliva, and you run on about what does not concern you. So be ashamed before God and before them)."

Al-Dahhak said: their place is under the lip, on the palate. Awf transmitted it from al-Hasan, who said: al-Hasan was pleased to keep his goatee clean.

As for His saying "qa'id" (sitting) rather than "qa'idan" (two sitting), though they are two, the reason is that the meaning is: "one on the right sitting, and one on the left sitting," so the first is omitted because the second indicates it. This was stated by Sibawayh, and from it is the poet's saying:

We are content with what we have, and you with what you have,
Though opinions differ.[[The poet is Qays ibn al-Khatim.]]

Al-Farazdaq said:

I guaranteed for whoever came to me what he committed,
And he refused, so it was, and I was not treacherous.

He did not say "radiyan" (both content) or "ghadurayn" (both treacherous). The view of al-Mubarrad is that the one mentioned in the recitation is the first, and the second is omitted because the first indicates it. The view of al-Akhfash and al-Farra' is that the one mentioned in the recitation expresses both the dual and the plural, and there is no omission in the speech. "Qa'id" means "qa'id" (sitting), like "sami'" (hearing), "'alim" (knowing), "qadir" (capable), and "shahid" (witness). It was also said: "qa'id" means "muqa'id" (one who sits with), like "akil" (one who eats with) and "nadim" (one who drinks with), meaning "mu'akil" (one who eats together) and "munadim" (one who drinks together). Al-Jawhari said: *fa'il* and *fa'ul* are forms that are used for the singular, dual, and plural alike, as in His saying: (We are the messenger of the Lord of the worlds).[[See vol. 13, p. 39.]]

And His saying: (And the angels after that are a support).[[See vol. 18, p. 191.]] Al-Tha'labi cited a poet using it for the plural:

Send me to her, and the best of messengers
Is the most knowledgeable of the ways of news.[[*Al-kanni ilayha*: send me to her. The original is *al-ki'na*, where the kasra was moved onto the lam and the hamza was dropped.]]

The word "qa'id" here means one who is constantly present and fixed, not the opposite of standing.

His saying, exalted is He: (Not a word does he utter but there is an observer beside him, ready). That is, he does not speak any word but it is recorded against him. It is derived from the word for food, meaning expelling it from the mouth. There are three views concerning *al-raqib* (the observer): first, that he is the one who follows matters; second, that he is the guardian, as stated by al-Suddi; third, that he is the witness, as stated by al-Dahhak. Concerning *al-'atid* (ready) there are two views: first, that he is the present one who does not leave; second, that he is the guardian prepared either for guarding or for testifying. Al-Jawhari said: *al-'atid* is the thing that is present and prepared; one says *'attadahu* (prepared it) *ta'tidan* and *a'taddahu i'tidadan*, meaning he prepared it for a day. From this is His saying: (And she prepared for them a couch).[[See vol. 9, p. 178.]] A horse that is *'atad* or *'atid* (with the *ta'* vowelled with fatha or kasra) is one prepared for running. I say: all of this returns to the meaning of presence, and from it is the poet's saying:

Even if you are absent from me in sight,
Your remembrance is with me in the heart, ready.

Abu al-Jawza' and Mujahid said: everything a person does is recorded, even his groaning in his illness. Ikrimah said: only what he is rewarded for or held accountable for is recorded. It was also said: everything he says is recorded, but at the end of the day what was permissible is erased, such as "Go," "Sit," "Eat," which carry neither reward nor sin. And God knows best.

It was transmitted from Abu Hurayrah and Anas that the Prophet ﷺ said: "There are no two guardians who raise to God what they have guarded, and God sees good at the beginning of the record and good at its end, but God says to His angels: 'Bear witness that I have forgiven My servant what is between the two edges of the record.'" Ali, may God be pleased with him, said: "God has angels with white scrolls. Write good at its beginning and at its end, and you will be forgiven what is between that."

Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz narrated to us, saying: Abu Tahir Muhammad ibn al-Fadl ibn Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Khuzaymah narrated to us, saying: my grandfather Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Harashi narrated to us, saying: Sahl ibn Abd Allah narrated to us, saying: I heard al-A'mash narrating from Zayd ibn Wahb, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "When the two guardians descend upon the servant, male or female, with a sealed book, they record what the servant utters. When they want to rise, one says to the other: 'Open the sealed book that is with you,' and he opens it for him, and in it is what they recorded, exactly the same. Abu Bakr said: "Why did you not say as God said: (And the agony of death came with truth; that is what you were trying to avoid)?" And he mentioned the hadith.

It was also narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Indeed the righteous servant struggles with death and its agonies, and his joints greet one another, saying: 'Peace be upon you; you part from me and I part from you until the Day of Resurrection.'"

It was also narrated: "Indeed death is harder than being struck with swords, sawn with saws, and cut with shears."

(That is what you used to shun.) That is, it is said to the one whose death-agony has come: "This is what you used to flee from and turn away from." It is said: "ḥāda 'an al-shay'" (he swerved from the thing), yaḥīdu, ḥuyūdan, ḥaydatan, and ḥaydūdatan, meaning he inclined away from it and deviated. Abā Mundhir, you wished to be faithful, so you feared it,
and you swerved as the camel swerves from the slippery ground.

And We created man, meaning mankind. It was also said that "man" refers to Adam.

(And We know what his soul whispers to him) That is, what stirs in his secret thoughts, his heart, and his inner self. This is a warning against the sins that a person commits in secret. Whoever says that "man" refers to Adam holds that what his soul whispered to him was eating from the tree, and then the meaning is general to his offspring. *Waswasah* (whispering) is the soul's talking to itself, like a hidden speech. Al-A'sha said:

You hear the jingling of ornaments as she turns away,
Like the rustle of the *'ishriq* (a plant) stirred by a wind.[[*'Ishriq* (*kaz* or *burj*): a plant that spreads over the ground with broad leaves and no thorns. This has already been discussed in (*al-A'raf*).[[See vol. 7, p. 177.]]

Is the most knowledgeable of the ways of news.[[*Al-kanni ilayha*: send me to her. The original is *al-ki'na*, where the kasra was moved onto the lam and the hamza was dropped.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 50, verses 20–22:

Allah's words: ﴿And the Horn will be blown﴾. It is the final blast for the Resurrection (ba'th). ﴿That is the Day of the Threat﴾, which Allah promised the disbelievers that He would punish them on that day. The discussion of the blowing of the Horn has already passed in full [see vol. 13, p. 239 and vol. 15, p. 279], and praise be to Allah.

Allah's words: ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness﴾. Scholars differed concerning the driver (sa'iq) and the witness (shahid). Ibn 'Abbas said: the driver is from the angels, and the witness is from among their own selves, the hands and the feet. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. Abu Hurayrah said: the driver is an angel, and the witness is the deed. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the meaning is a driver who drives it and a witness who testifies against it concerning its deeds. Ibn Muslim said: the driver is its companion from the devils; he is called a driver because he follows it, even if he does not urge it. Mujahid said: the driver and the witness are two angels. It is related from 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said while on the pulpit: ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness﴾. The driver: an angel who drives it to the command of Allah; and the witness: one who testifies against it concerning its deeds.

I (al-Qurtubi) say: This is the most sound view, for in the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed, the son of Adam is in heedlessness of what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has created for him. There is no god but Him. When He wills to create him, He says to the angel: Write his provision, his effects, his term, and write him as wretched or happy. Then that angel ascends, and Allah sends another angel who guards him until he reaches maturity. Then Allah sends two angels who record his good deeds and his bad deeds. When death comes to him, those two angels ascend, then the angel of death, peace be upon him, comes and seizes his soul. When he enters his grave, the soul is returned to his body. Then the angel of death ascends. Then the two angels of the grave come to him and test him, then they ascend. When the Hour is established, the angel of good deeds and the angel of bad deeds descend upon him, and they unfasten a book bound upon his neck [[unfasten: to loosen its knot]]; then they come with him, one a driver and the other a witness. Then Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Certainly you were in heedlessness of this, so We have removed from you your covering, and your sight today is sharp﴾." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You will surely ride from stage to stage" [meaning: state after state]. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Before you is a grave matter, so seek help in Allah, the Mighty." Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz recorded it from the hadith of Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn 'Ali from Jabir, and said concerning it: This is a strange (gharib) hadith from the narration of Ja'far, and the hadith of Jabir was transmitted solely by Jabir al-Ju'fi, and from him al-Mufaddal.

Then regarding the verse there are two views: one is that it is general, applying to both the Muslim and the disbeliever, and this is the view of the majority. The second is that it is specific to the disbeliever, said by al-Dahhak.

Allah's words: ﴿Certainly you were in heedlessness of this, so We have removed from you your covering﴾. Ibn Zayd said: what is meant is the Prophet (ﷺ), i.e., "Certainly you were, O Muhammad, in heedlessness of the message among the Quraysh in their jahiliyyah." Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: what is meant is the polytheists, i.e., they were in heedlessness of the consequences of their affairs. Most of the exegetes said: what is meant is the righteous and the wicked. This is the choice of al-Tabari. It was also said: i.e., "Certainly you were, O human, in heedlessness of the fact that every soul will come with a driver and a witness, because this is known only through divine texts."

﴿So We have removed from you your covering﴾, i.e., your blindness. In it there are four interpretations: first, when he was in his mother's womb and then was born; this was said by al-Suddi. Second, when he was in the grave and then was raised; this is the meaning of the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. Third, the time of the presentation on the Day of Resurrection; this was said by Mujahid. Fourth, it is the descent of revelation and the bearing of the message; this is the meaning of the statement of Ibn Zayd.

﴿Your sight today is sharp﴾. It was said: what is meant is the sight of the heart, as one says "he is perceptive (basir) in jurisprudence," so the sight of the heart and its insight is its perception of the evidences of thoughts and the results of reflection, just as the eye perceives what is before it of persons and bodies. It was also said: what is meant is the sight of the eye, and this is the apparent meaning, i.e., the sight of your eye today is sharp, meaning strong and penetrating, seeing what was hidden from you. Mujahid said: ﴿your sight today is sharp﴾ means your gaze upon the tongue of your scale when your bad and good deeds are weighed. This was also said by al-Dahhak. It was said: he will witness what he will reach of reward and punishment; this is the meaning of the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: meaning that the disbeliever is raised while his sight is sharp, then he will turn blue and become blind. It is also recited as (لَقَدْ كُنْتَ), (عَنْكَ), (فَبَصَرُكَ) with kasra, addressing the soul (nafs).

The Almighty's words: ﴿On the Day We say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾ Nafi' and Abu Bakr read (yawma yaqulu) with the letter ya', taking the verb as referring back to His words, ﴿Do not dispute before Me﴾. The rest read it with nun, as address from God Most High, and this is the nun of greatness [[In ن and هـ: "the nun of exalting (al-ta'zim)."]]. Al-Hasan read (yawma aqulu). It is also reported from Ibn Mas'ud and others as (yawma yuqalu). (Yawma) is in the accusative, meaning: "the speech is not changed before Me on that Day." It has also been said that it is governed by a verb understood, meaning: "And warn them (on the Day We say to Hell, 'Are you filled?')," in accordance with His promise to her that He would fill her. This question is asked to affirm His report, to confirm His promise, to rebuke His enemies, and to alert all His servants.

(And Hell says) (Is there any more?), that is, there is no place left in me for more. This is like the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Has 'Aqil left us any dwelling or house?" meaning: he has left none. So the sense of the statement is denial. It may also be a question seeking more: "Is there any more, so that I may increase?" This works for both meanings, because a question carries a kind of denial. It has also been said: there is no actual speech, but it is a figure of speech, meaning that Hell, in its apparent condition, is like one speaking thus, as the poet said:

The basin is full and says, "Enough, slowly! You have filled my belly."

This is the interpretation of Mujahid and others, meaning: "Is there any place in me left unfilled?" It has also been said: God makes the Fire speak until it says this, just as the limbs speak. This is more sound according to what we have explained in Surat al-Furqan [[See vol. 13, p. 10.]]. In the Sahih of Muslim, al-Bukhari and al-Tirmidhi, from Anas ibn Malik, from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "Hell will not cease to have people cast into it, and it will say, 'Is there any more?' until the Lord of Might places His foot in it, and then part of it draws in toward part, and it says, 'Enough, enough, by Your might and Your generosity.' And Paradise will not cease to have room, until God creates for it a creation who will dwell in the extra room of Paradise." This is the wording of Muslim. In another narration from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "As for the Fire, it will not be filled until God places His foot upon it, and it says, 'Enough, enough,' and then it is filled, and part of it draws in toward part, and God does not wrong any of His creatures. As for Paradise, God creates for it a creation."

Our scholars, may God have mercy on them, said: As for the meaning of "foot" here, it refers to a people whom God sends forward to the Fire, and it had already been foreknown in His knowledge that they are among the people of the Fire. Likewise "rijl," which means a large number of people and others. It is said: "I saw a rijl of people and a rijl of locusts." The poet said:

A rijl of people passed by us and gathered toward them from the Yemeni tribe are rijl [troops].

Tribes from Lakhm, 'Akk and Himyar, against the two sons of Nizar, eager for enmity.

What clarifies this meaning is what is related from Ibn Mas'ud, that he said: "There is in the Fire no house, no chain, no iron gag, and no coffin, except that it bears the name of its owner. Each of the guardians waits for his companion whose name and description he knows. When each of them has completed what he was commanded and what he awaits, and none is left, the guardians say, 'Enough, enough, it is sufficient for us, it is sufficient for us,' that is, 'we are satisfied, we are satisfied.' At that time Hell draws in over those in it and closes, since no one remains who is awaited." So that awaited gathering is expressed by "rijl" and "qadam." This interpretation is supported by his saying in the same hadith: "And Paradise will not cease to have room, until God creates for it a creation who will dwell in the extra room of Paradise." We have expanded on this meaning and clarified it in the book of the Names and Attributes from the book al-Asna, and praise belongs to God. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said, concerning the Prophet's saying, peace be upon him, "until the Tyrant places His foot in it," that it means: whoever was foreknown in His knowledge to be among the people of the Fire.

The Almighty's words: ﴿And Paradise is brought near for the God-fearing, not far off﴾. That is, it is brought close to them. It has been said: this is before entering the world, meaning it was brought near to their hearts when they were told to avoid sins. It has also been said: after entering, its places are brought near for them so that they are not far away.

(Not far off) means: not far from them, and this is emphasis.

(This is what you are promised) means: it will be said to them, "This is the reward you were promised in the world through the tongues of the messengers." The common reading is (tu'adun) with ta', as address. Ibn Kathir read it with ya', as a report, because it came after the mention of the God-fearing.

(For every penitent, keeper [of covenant]) — (awwab) means one who returns to God from sins, then returns to sin, then returns again. This is what al-Dahhak and others said. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' said: the awwab is the one who glorifies God, from His saying: ﴿O mountains, echo His praise with him﴾ [[See vol. 14, p. 264.]]. Al-Hakam ibn 'Utaybah said: he is the one who remembers God in privacy. Al-Sha'bi and Mujahid said: he is the one who recalls his sins in privacy and then seeks God's forgiveness for them. This is also the saying of Ibn Mas'ud. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: he is the one who does not sit in a gathering until he seeks God's forgiveness in it. He also said: "We used to be told that the awwab keeper is the one who, when he rises from his gathering, says: 'Glory be to God and praise be to Him. O God, I seek Your forgiveness for what I did in this gathering of mine.'" And in a hadith: "Whoever says when he rises from his gathering, 'Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You. There is no god but You. I seek Your forgiveness and turn to You,' God forgives him for what was in that gathering." And thus the Prophet ﷺ used to say. Some scholars said: "I prefer to say, 'I seek Your forgiveness and ask You for repentance,' and I do not like to say 'and I turn to You' except in its true sense." I say: This is a personal preference, and following the hadith is better. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: he is the one who relies upon God in ease and hardship. Al-Qasim said: he is the one who occupies himself with none but God, Mighty and Majestic.

(Keeper) — Ibn 'Abbas said: he is the one who guards his sins until he turns away from them. Qatadah said: he guards what God has entrusted to him of His right and His blessing, and what He has made him trustworthy in. It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas: he is the one who guards God's command. Mujahid said: he is the one who guards God's right through acknowledgment and His blessings through thankfulness. Al-Dahhak said: he is the one who guards God's command by accepting it. Makhul narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever observes four rak'ahs at the beginning of the day is an awwab keeper." Al-Mawardi mentioned it.

The Almighty's words: ﴿Who fears the Most Merciful in the unseen﴾. (Man) is in the genitive position as a substitute for His words, "for every penitent keeper," or in the position of an adjective for (awwab). It is permissible to read it in the nominative as a new sentence, with the predicate being (enter it), and the condition's answer omitted, the sense being: "it will be said to them, 'Enter it.'" Fear in the unseen means that you fear Him while you have not seen Him. Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: this means in privacy, when no one sees him. Al-Hasan said: when he lets down the curtain and closes the door.

(And comes with a contrite heart) — turning in obedience. It has also been said: sincere. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: the sign of the contrite one is that he knows the sanctity of God and is devoted to Him, humble before His majesty, and abandons the desires of his soul. I say: The contrite heart may also be the sound heart, as He said: ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 114.]], as mentioned earlier, and God knows best.

(Enter it) — that is, it will be said to the people of these attributes: ﴿Enter it in peace; that is the Day of Eternity﴾, that is, in safety from punishment. It has also been said: in peace from God and His angels upon them. It has also been said: in safety from the loss of blessings. He said "enter it" while the beginning of the speech was "whoever feared," because (man) can carry the meaning of plurality.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿For them is whatever they wish therein﴾, meaning whatever their souls desire and their eyes delight in.

(And with Us is more) — of blessings, things that never occurred to their minds. Anas and Jabir said: the "more" is looking at the face of God Most High without how. This has been reported in reports traced back to the Prophet ﷺ regarding His saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best reward﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 330.]] (and more). He said: the "more" is looking at the noble face of God. Ibn al-Mubarak and Yahya ibn Sallam both mentioned, saying: al-Mas'udi informed us, from al-Minhal ibn 'Amr, from Abu 'Ubaydah ibn 'Abdullah ibn 'Utbah, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Hasten to the Friday prayer, for God, blessed and exalted, manifests Himself to the people of Paradise every Friday on a white mound of camphor, and they are near to Him." Ibn al-Mubarak said: according to the measure of their haste to the Friday prayer in the world. Yahya ibn Sallam said: because of their hastening to the congregations in the world. He added: "So God brings about for them a honor they had not seen before." Yahya said: I heard someone other than al-Mas'udi add to it the words of His Exalted saying: ﴿And with Us is more﴾.

I say: His saying "on a mound" refers to the people of Paradise, meaning that they are on mounds, as in the mursal of al-Hasan, who said: the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The people of Paradise look at their Lord every Friday from a mound of camphor," and the hadith continues. **Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 50, verses 36–38:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿How many generations We destroyed before them who were far mightier in strength than they﴾. That is, how many nations, O Muhammad, did We destroy before your people, nations that were mightier than them in force and power.

(﴿Then they roamed through the lands﴾) means they travelled through them seeking a place of escape. It is also said: they left their mark on the lands, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Mujahid said: they struck and wandered about. al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: they went round. Qatadah said: they traversed. al-Mu'arrij said: they went far away. From this is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*"I have searched the horizons until I was content to return instead of gaining spoils."*

Then it was said: they wandered to the remote parts of the lands seeking trade, and did they find any escape from death? It is also said: they wandered through the lands seeking a way of escape from death. al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

*"They searched the lands out of fear of death, and roamed the earth in every passage."*

al-Hasan and Abu al-Aliyah recited (*fa-naqabu*) with a fatha on the qaf and with light emphasis (*takhfif*). *Al-naqb* is the piercing and entering into a thing. It is also said: *al-naqb* is a path through a mountain, and likewise *al-manqab* and *al-manqabah*, from Ibn al-Sikkit. One says *naqaba al-jidar naqban* (he pierced the wall), and the name of that opening is also *naqb*, and the plural of *al-naqb* is *al-nuqub*; that is, they cut through the lands and travelled through their passages. It is also said: they left their mark on them like the iron's mark on what it pierces.

Yahya ibn Ya'mur al-Sulami recited (*fa-naqqibu*) with a kasra on the qaf and emphasis (*tashdid*), as an imperative of threat and warning, meaning: roam the lands, travel through them, and look: is there (*hal min*) any escape (*mahis*) from death? This is reported by al-Tha'labi. al-Qushayri related (*fa-naqibu*) with a kasra on the qaf and light emphasis, meaning: they travelled through them so much that their beasts became worn out. al-Jawhari said: the camel's hooves became "*naqiba*" (*naqiba*, worn through) when they became thin, and a man became "*anqaba*" when his camel was worn; and a worn shoe became "*naqiba*," that is, torn.

*Al-Mahis* is a verbal noun from *haasa 'anhu yahisu hayصan* and *huyuusan* and *mahisan* and *mahasan* and *hayasanan*, meaning he deviated and swerved. One says: *ma 'anhu mahis*, meaning there is no escape or refuge from it. *Al-inyiyas* has the same meaning. One says of allies: they swerved away from the enemy; and of enemies: they were routed.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder﴾, that is, in what We have mentioned in this surah there is a reminder and an admonition (﴿for whoever has a heart﴾), that is, an intellect by which he reflects. The heart is used here to mean the intellect because it is its seat. Mujahid and others said this. It is also said: for whoever has life and a discerning soul. The living soul is expressed by the heart because it is the soul's home and the source of its life, as Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Has my love deceived you, that your love is my killer, and that whatever you command the heart, it does?"*

In the revelation: ﴿That it may warn whoever is alive﴾. Yahya ibn Mu'adh said: there are two hearts. A heart filled with the concerns of this world, so that when a matter of the Hereafter arrives, it does not know what to do; and a heart filled with the terrors of the Hereafter, so that when a matter of this world arrives, it does not know what to do, because its heart has gone to the Hereafter.

(﴿Or gives ear﴾), that is, listens to the Qur'an. The Arabs say: *alqi ilayya sam'aka*, meaning listen to me. The manner of listening and its fruit have already been discussed in Surah Ta-Ha.

(﴿And he is a witness﴾), that is, a witness with the heart. al-Zajjaj said: that is, his heart is present in what he hears. Sufyan said: that is, he is not present while his heart is absent.

Then it was said: this verse concerns the People of the Book, as Mujahid and Qatadah said. al-Hasan said: it refers specifically to the Jews and Christians. Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Abu Salih said: it refers specifically to the people of the Qur'an.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 50, verses 39–40:**

There are five issues in this passage.

The first concerns God's words: ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾. This is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), commanding him to be patient with what the polytheists say, meaning: make their matter easy for you. It was revealed before the command to fight, so it is abrogated (mansukh). It was said: it is established (muhkam) for the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community. It was also said that its meaning is: be patient over what the Jews say, that God rested on the Sabbath.

The second concerns God's words: ﴿And glorify your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting﴾. It was said that He intended by this the five prayers. Abu Salih said: "Before the rising of the sun" is the Dawn prayer (Subh), and "before the setting" is the Afternoon prayer ('Asr). Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah related it as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ) report. He said: "We were sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ) when he looked at the moon on the night of the full moon and said: 'Indeed you will see your Lord just as you see this moon; you will not be wronged in seeing Him. So if you are able not to be overcome in a prayer before the rising of the sun and before its setting, then do so,' meaning the 'Asr and the Fajr." Then Jarir recited: ﴿And glorify your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting﴾. [[See vol. 11, p. 261.]] (Agreed upon by al-Bukhari and Muslim; the wording is Muslim's.) Ibn 'Abbas said: "before the setting" refers to the Zuhr and the 'Asr.

﴿And glorify Him during part of the night﴾ means the two night prayers ('Isha'ayn). It was also said: the meaning is glorifying Him verbally, declaring Him free of imperfection, before the rising of the sun and before its setting. This was said by 'Ata' al-Khurasani and Abu al-Ahwas. Some scholars, regarding His words "before the rising of the sun," said: it is the two rak'ahs of Fajr; and "before the setting" is the two rak'ahs before Maghrib. Thumama ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Anas said: the people of understanding among the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) used to pray the two rak'ahs before Maghrib.

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Anas ibn Malik, he said: "We were in Medina; when the caller (mu'adhdhin) called for the Maghrib prayer, they hastened to the pillars [[Ibtadaru al-sawari: they hastened to them; al-sawari is the plural of al-sariya, meaning the pillar. That is, each worshipper would stand behind a pillar so that no one would pass in front of him while praying alone.]] and prayed two rak'ahs, so much so that a stranger would enter the mosque and think the prayer had already been performed because of how many were praying them." Qatada said: "I did not meet anyone who prayed the two rak'ahs except Anas and Abu Barza al-Aslami."

The third issue concerns God's words: ﴿And during part of the night glorify Him, and at the ends of the prostrations﴾. There are four opinions concerning it.
The first: it is glorifying God during the night. Abu al-Ahwas said this.
The second: it is the whole night prayer. Mujahid said this.
The third: it is the two rak'ahs of Fajr. Ibn 'Abbas said this.
The fourth: it is the late 'Isha' prayer. Ibn Zayd said this.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: whoever says that it is glorifying in the night, the sound (hadith) supports him: "Whoever wakes up (ta'arra) [[Ta'arra: he awakens.]] during the night and says: 'There is no god but God alone, with no partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs praise, and He is over all things capable. Glory be to God, praise be to God, there is no god but God, God is greatest, and there is no power nor strength except by God, the Exalted, the Mighty.'" As for whoever says it is the prayer at night, prayer is called tasbih because it contains the glorification of God, and from this comes the "subhat al-Duha" (the forenoon prayer). As for whoever says it is the Fajr or 'Isha' prayer, it is because these two are part of the night prayer, and 'Isha' is more evident in this.

The fourth issue concerns God's words: ﴿and at the ends of the prostrations﴾. 'Umar, 'Ali, Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, al-Awza'i and al-Zuhri said: "The ends of the prostrations" are the two rak'ahs after Maghrib, and "the ends of the stars" are the two rak'ahs before Fajr. Al-'Awfi related it from Ibn 'Abbas, and he raised it (to the Prophet ﷺ). Ibn 'Abbas said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Two rak'ahs after Maghrib are the ends of the prostrations." Al-Tha'labi mentioned it. The wording of al-Mawardi is: It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "I spent a night with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he prayed two rak'ahs before Fajr, then he went out to the prayer and said: 'O Ibn 'Abbas, two rak'ahs before Fajr are the ends of the stars, and two rak'ahs after Maghrib are the ends of the prostrations.'"

Anas said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever prays two rak'ahs after Maghrib before speaking, his prayer will be written in 'Illiyyin." Anas said: "In the first rak'ah he recited: ﴿Say: O disbelievers﴾, and in the second: ﴿Say: He is God, One﴾." Muqatil said: its time lasts as long as the red twilight (al-shafaq al-ahmar) has not disappeared.

It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas: "It is the witr (odd-numbered prayer)." Ibn Zayd said: "It is the voluntary prayers after the obligatory prayers, two rak'ahs after each obligatory prayer." Al-Nahhas said: the apparent meaning supports this, though it is better to follow the majority, and this is authentic from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him. Abu al-Ahwas said: "It is glorifying in the ends of the prostrations." Ibn al-'Arabi said: this is the strongest in reasoning.

In the authentic hadith: the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say after the obligatory prayer: "There is no god but God alone, with no partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs praise, and He is over all things capable. O God, there is none who can withhold what You give, and none who can give what You withhold, and the wealth of the wealthy will not benefit them against You [[Wa la yanfa'u dha al-jadd minka al-jadd: meaning the wealthy person's wealth does not benefit him before You; only faith and obedience benefit him. (Al-Nihaya by Ibn al-Athir.)]]." It was said that it is abrogated by the obligatory duties, so none is obligated except the five prayers; the group (of scholars) transmitted this.

The fifth issue: Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Hamza recited ﴿wa-idbara al-sujud﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, as a verbal noun (masdar) of adbara al-shay'u idbaran, meaning "it turned away." The rest recited it with a fatha, as the plural of dubur. This is the recitation of 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas. Its pattern is like tunub and atnab, or dubr like qufl and aqfal. They used it as an adverb of time, as in "I came to you after (dubur) the prayer" and "after (adbar) the prayer." There is no disagreement concerning the end of (Surat al-Tur).

As for ﴿wa-idbara al-nujum﴾, with the kasra it is a verbal noun, meaning the going away of their light when the second dawn rises, which is the whiteness that splits the blackness of the night.

**The Qur'an: "And listen on the Day when the Caller calls from a nearby place"** (50:41). The object of "listen" is omitted, meaning: listen to the call, the voice, or the Blast (al-sayhah), which is the Blast of the Resurrection. This is the second blowing of the Trumpet. The Caller is Jibril (Gabriel). It is also said that the Caller is Israfil (Seraphiel).

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also said that Israfil blows and Jibril calls out. He calls for the gathering and says: "Come to the reckoning." On this view, the calling takes place at the place of assembly (al-mahshar).

It is also said: "Listen to the calling of the disbelievers, crying 'Woe!' and 'Destruction!', from a nearby place." That is, everyone hears it, and no one is far from that call. Ikrimah said: The Caller of the All-Merciful calls, as if He were calling into their ears.

It is also said: the nearby place is the Rock of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It is said that it is the center of the earth and the nearest part of the earth to the heaven, by twelve miles. Ka'b said: by eighteen miles. Al-Qushayri and al-Zamakhshari mentioned the first figure, and al-Mawardi the second.

Jibril or Israfil stands on the Rock and calls for the gathering: "O decayed bones! O scattered joints! O crumbling bones! O perished shrouds! O empty hearts! O corrupted bodies! O flowing eyes! Qatadah used to say: "O God, make us of those who fear Your warning and hope for Your promise." Ya'qub kept the yā' in "wa‘idi" in both states, Warsh kept it in continuation but not in pause, and the rest omitted it in both states.

And God knows best. The commentary on Surat Qaf is complete, and praise be to God.

**The Qur'an: "And listen on the Day when the Caller calls from a nearby place"** (50:41). The object of "listen" is omitted, meaning: listen to the call, the voice, or the Blast (al-sayhah), which is the Blast of the Resurrection. This is the second blowing of the Trumpet. The Caller is Jibril (Gabriel). It is also said that the Caller is Israfil (Seraphiel).

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also said that Israfil blows and Jibril calls out. He calls for the gathering and says: "Come to the reckoning." On this view, the calling takes place at the place of assembly (al-mahshar).

It is also said: "Listen to the calling of the disbelievers, crying 'Woe!' and 'Destruction!', from a nearby place." That is, everyone hears it, and no one is far from that call. Ikrimah said: The Caller of the All-Merciful calls, as if He were calling into their ears.

It is also said: the nearby place is the Rock of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It is said that it is the center of the earth and the nearest part of the earth to the heaven, by twelve miles. Ka'b said: by eighteen miles. Al-Qushayri and al-Zamakhshari mentioned the first figure, and al-Mawardi the second.

Jibril or Israfil stands on the Rock and calls for the gathering: "O decayed bones! O scattered joints! O crumbling bones! O perished shrouds! O empty hearts! O corrupted bodies! O flowing eyes! Rise for the presentation before the Lord of the worlds." Qatadah said: It is Israfil, the bearer of the Trumpet (Sur).

**The Qur'an: "The Day they hear the Blast in truth; that is the Day of Coming Forth"** (50:42). "The Blast" means the Blast of Resurrection. The meaning of "coming forth" (al-khuruj) is the gathering for the reckoning.

**The Qur'an: "That is the Day of Coming Forth"** (50:42). That is, the Day of coming forth from the graves.

**The Qur'an: "Indeed We, it is We who give life and cause death"** (50:43). We cause the living to die and We bring the dead to life. Here the reality is affirmed.

**The Qur'an: "The Day the earth splits open over them, hastening"** (50:44). They hasten toward the Caller, the bearer of the Trumpet, toward Bayt al-Maqdis.

**The Qur'an: "That is a gathering easy for Us"** (50:44). That is, easy and simple.

The Kufans recited "tashaqqaqu" with the shin lightened, by omitting the first ta'. The rest recited it with the ta' assimilated into the shin. Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub kept the yā' of "al-munadi" (the Caller) in both pause and continuation, as in the original form. Nafi' and Abu Amr kept it only in continuation. The rest omitted it in both states.

I say: The Sunnah has added explanation to this verse. Al-Tirmidhi related from Mu'awiya ibn Haydah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), in a hadith he mentioned, who said: He pointed with his hand toward al-Sham (Syria) and said: "From here to here you will be gathered, riding and on foot, and on the Day of Resurrection you will be dragged upon your faces, with a gag upon your mouths. You will be seventy nations, and you are the best of them and the most honored of them before God. The first part of any of you to speak (to testify) will be his thigh," and in another narration, "his thigh and his palm."

Ali ibn Ma'bad related from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), in a hadith he mentioned: Then He—meaning God, exalted is He—says to Israfil: "Blow the blast of Resurrection." He blows, and the spirits come forth like swarms of bees, filling what is between the heaven and the earth. Then God, mighty and majestic, says: "By My might and My majesty, every spirit shall return to its body." The spirits enter the earth to the bodies, then they enter the nostrils, and move through the bodies like poison through the one stung. Then the earth splits open over you, and I am the first whom the earth splits open for. You come forth from it as youths, all of you aged thirty-three, and the tongue on that day is Syriac. And he mentioned the hadith.

We have mentioned all of this and more in full in *al-Tadhkirah*, and praise be to God.

**The Qur'an: "We know best what they say"** (50:45). That is, of your denial and of your reviling.

**The Qur'an: "And you are not over them a compeller"** (50:45). That is, a ruler who forces them to Islam. On this reading the verse is abrogated (mansukhah, i.e., its ruling is replaced by a later one, naskh) by the command to fight. "Jabbar" comes from compulsion and domination, since it is not said that "jabbar" means "one who compels," just as "kharraj" is not said to mean "one who causes to go out." This was related by al-Qushayri.

Al-Nahhas said: It is also said that the meaning of "jabbar" is "you do not compel them." This is an error, because "fa'‘al" does not come from "af‘al."

Al-Tha'labi related: Tha'lab said: Forms of the pattern "fa''al" have come with the meaning of "muf‘il," and they are rare: "jabbar" meaning "mujbir" (compeller), "darrak" meaning "mudrik" (one who overtakes), "sarra'" meaning "musri'" (hasty), "bakka'" meaning "mubki" (causing to weep), and "addā'" meaning "mu‘addi" (one who causes to run).

It has been recited, "wa ma ahdakum illa sabila al-rashshad" (Q. 40:38), with the shin doubled, meaning "al-murshid" (the guide), and this is Musa. It is also said that it is God.

Likewise it has been recited, "amma al-safinatu fa-kanat limasakin" (Q. 18:79), meaning "mumsikin" (holders-fast). Abu Hamid al-Kharazinji said: The Arabs say: "sayf saqqat" (a sword that cuts down), meaning "musqit" (one that causes to fall).

It is also said: "bi-jabbar" means "bi-musaytir" (overseer), as in Surat al-Ghashiyah: "You are not over them a dominator" (Q. 88:22).

Al-Farra' said: I heard from the Arabs one who says: "jabarahu ‘ala al-amr," meaning "qahara-hu" (he overpowered him). So "jabbar" in this dialect means "one who overpowers," and this is sound. It is said: "jabbar" comes from their saying "jabartuhu ‘ala al-amr," meaning "ajbartuhu" (I compelled him), and this is a Kinanah dialect; the two are two forms of the same usage.

Al-Jawhari said: "Ajbartuhu ‘ala al-amr" means "akrahtuhu ‘alayhi" (I forced him to it). "Ajbartuhu" also means "I attributed him to al-jabr (compulsion)," just as you say "akfartuhu" when you attribute him to disbelief.

**The Qur'an: "So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning"** (50:45). Ibn ‘Abbas said: They said: "O Messenger of God, if only you would frighten us!" So this was revealed: "So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning." That is, what I have prepared of punishment for whoever disobeys Me. So "al-wa‘id" is punishment, and "al-wa‘d" is reward. *"And though I threaten him or promise him, I break my threat and fulfill my promise."*
